feedback.advice: Before the formalization note, ask for a short teach-back: why two routes can reveal the plant, why few queries rarely take either route, and why cheap comparisons avoid checking every candidate. Keep it as a comprehension task rather than a replacement conclusion.

locator.quote: A good place to begin is the second clause of the winning condition

feedback.feedback: This turns formalization into a concrete reading action tied to the changed board, rather than asking me to trust a large certification claim. I know what the clause should exclude and can compare that meaning with the statement.
feedback.why_it_matters: It gives a non-Lean mathematician a useful task without making them learn the proof implementation.
feedback.advice: Keep this example-based invitation and the readable definition links. It is the right pattern for the closing formalization section.

locator.quote: We give the complete argument with explicit constants

feedback.feedback: Complete argument suggests a self-contained proof, but the last paragraph of the introduction lists several accepted inputs and later §5 cites a substantial independent proof from the record. Those are defensible choices for a companion, yet the compact scope qualification arrives much later than the promise.
feedback.why_it_matters: A newcomer choosing between the companion and record cannot predict which proof they will actually find here.
feedback.advice: Describe the companion’s scope consistently at the abstract and reading-route level: the construction and both main analyses are supplied, with the named standard or supplier results accepted. This is a scope adjustment, not a request to duplicate the record.

locator.quote: There are total Boolean functions $F$ with $R(F)\ge Q(F)^{4-o(1)}$

feedback.feedback: After the exposition’s careful fixed-k warning, the abstract immediately uses the stronger-looking single-family shorthand. The later growing-k remark does justify it, but the first line does not tell a returning newcomer where that quantifier change is accounted for.
feedback.why_it_matters: The two derived documents can appear to disagree about whether k may vary.
feedback.advice: Give the o(1) claim a short pointer to the growing-k remark or distinguish it from the fixed-k headline when discussing what the companion adds. Do not weaken or strengthen the theorem.

locator.quote: a tournament whose comparisons need to be reliable only for the winner

feedback.feedback: After the exposition I understand this mechanism, but the abstract does not point me to the short account of the invariant or final verification. For a returning learner, the specialized paper needs a small navigational bridge keyed to the concepts just learned.
feedback.why_it_matters: I can recognize the slogan but must reread the whole introduction to locate the proof I came to check.
feedback.advice: In the existing roadmap, name the weight-halving identity and retained candidate list alongside the section number. Do not make the abstract longer with a second proof overview.

locator.quote: A query algorithm reads its input one bit at a time

feedback.feedback: As a general opening about both models, this invites the classical picture of a revealed single bit. The next sentences correctly introduce quantum oracle access, but my initial picture needs an immediate repair.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader can confuse counting one oracle call with learning one chosen classical input bit.
feedback.advice: Make the first sentence explicitly about classical access or describe the common charged resource before specifying the two access rules. The specialist paper needs only a small precision edit.

locator.quote: The constant $C_\alpha$ is uniform in $n$ and $f$

feedback.feedback: This short explanation resolves the essential quantifier question in the definition of the exponent. It is much more useful than a generic reminder that asymptotic constants exist.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without uniformity over functions, the meaning of a universal exponent is easy to misread.
feedback.advice: Keep it next to the definition and carry the same verbal explanation into the exposition when that definition is first used.

locator.quote: $b_k$

feedback.feedback: Theorem 1 introduces an unspecified logarithmic exponent b_k, although the very next contribution paragraph says it is six and §3 proves that choice. This is mathematically harmless but gives me another parameter to remember without explaining why the theorem is being stated at the weaker level.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader may conflate the general preprint statement, the explicit paper estimate and the existential formal statement.
feedback.advice: Explain the choice of theorem granularity once, or use the explicit bound in the principal displayed statement and reserve the existential variant for the correspondence discussion. Do not change the mathematical result.

locator.quote: First, the constants are explicit:

feedback.feedback: The contribution sentence contains four unrelated numerical refinements, several section references, a size parameter change and the same-circuit condition. The mechanism and the relation to the preprint are more important to the reader than a single encounter with 2^53 or 13669.
feedback.why_it_matters: The first account of what this companion contributes reads as an inventory rather than a claim about how the proof becomes clearer.
feedback.advice: Group the refinements by purpose and let the exact large constants live where their bounds are used. Retain the shared-circuit point, but give it its own short logical role rather than attaching it to the list of numbers. Distinguish constants that establish parameter uniformity from deliberately loose accounting constants.

locator.quote: $R=\widetilde\Omega(Q^{5/2})$

feedback.feedback: Tilde notation appears before the companion states what it suppresses. A mathematician from another field may know O and Omega but not whether the tilde hides logarithms in input length, Q, or both, or whether k-dependent constants are allowed.
feedback.why_it_matters: The history is a comparison of powers, so the precise convention matters more here than it would in an incidental estimate.
feedback.advice: Give one short convention for suppressed logarithmic factors and fixed construction parameters. Link an explanation for the newcomer rather than expanding every historical statement.

locator.quote: the AND–OR recipe stops at the cube

feedback.feedback: The sentence correctly confines the cubic barrier to a specific construction recipe. The preceding formulas show where the two factors from AND–OR and the one factor from the partial function enter.
feedback.why_it_matters: It avoids mistaking a limitation of a method for a theorem that all total functions satisfy a cubic bound.
feedback.advice: Keep this qualification and the old-versus-new exponent arithmetic. It is a useful contrast to the new tournament mechanism, not history for its own sake.

locator.quote: Tal's bound for $k$-fold Rorrelation

feedback.feedback: Rorrelation first looks like a typographical error in Forrelation. Only the later relation-to-constructions section explains the random orthogonal matrix variant.
feedback.why_it_matters: I may silently normalize the names and miss why the explicit Walsh form is important for the circuit construction.
feedback.advice: At the first occurrence, identify Rorrelation as the random-orthogonal-matrix variant. This is a terminology bridge, not a request to reproduce its lower-bound proof.

locator.quote: Exponent $a$ with $R=Q^{a}$ (total $f$)

feedback.feedback: The table heading uses equality, while its rows mix achievable lower-bound separations, logarithmic or o(1) losses, and one universal upper bound. The prose distinguishes these directions, but the table erases them precisely where I am trying to compare the landscape.
feedback.why_it_matters: A quick reader could report a matching exact power relation for a particular family, or regard the final upper-bound row as another construction.
feedback.advice: Label achieved separations and universal limitations separately, and state the bound direction in the header or each row. Keep the compact historical comparison.

locator.quote: Finding the erased zero means finding one marked zero among $m$ columns

feedback.feedback: There are m hidden zeros in the dummy board, and one is erased in the planted board. The phrase one marked zero can make me imagine a single marked item in an otherwise uniform m-by-m array, which is a different distribution.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader then misses why the identity involving the expected number of discovered zeros, and independence of the selected column, are the right proof tools.
feedback.advice: State the two levels of hiding: one zero per column, followed by an independent choice of the column whose zero will be changed. The later planting diagram already illustrates the correct experiment.

locator.quote: $L\approx R(P)\approx m^{1-1/k}$

feedback.feedback: L is a chosen lower-bound threshold and the proof later needs only L<R(P). The approximation chain reads as an asymptotic characterization of R(P), although no matching upper bound is stated here and the logarithmic convention is implicit.
feedback.why_it_matters: It can make the lower-bound mechanism seem to rely on more information about the partial function than is actually needed.
feedback.advice: Describe L as the usable hardness scale, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Keep the rigorous one-sided role visible instead of suggesting that the proof needs equality with the true randomized complexity.

locator.quote: The winner's guarantee does not depend on the rival's address inputs

feedback.feedback: This is the right robust-quantum-algorithm insight to carry out of the exposition. It says why off-promise labels of losing columns can be tolerated and how the pointer direction produces the one-sided reliability actually used.
feedback.why_it_matters: It connects the totality requirement directly to the unusual tournament assumption.
feedback.advice: Keep this explanation before the abstract proposition. It is more instructive than describing the comparison merely as bounded error.

locator.quote: In $F_{k,m}$ a zero carries no pointer.

feedback.feedback: This is a concise, concrete comparison with the predecessor construction. It explains why finding a zero does not immediately reveal the winning column, and why the location of the pointer data matters to the lower bound.
feedback.why_it_matters: The attribution teaches a design constraint rather than adding a list of names.
feedback.advice: Preserve this sentence and the explanation of separately stored pointer fields. It is one of the strongest parts of the related-work discussion.

locator.quote: king finding

feedback.feedback: King finding, sink and fixed tournament appear in a paragraph that is supposed to explain the closest antecedents. I know graph theory but not the specialized search target, so I cannot tell whether the new algorithm is finding the same object under weaker comparisons.
feedback.why_it_matters: A short unexplained term can conceal the substantive difference between the searches.
feedback.advice: Add a brief parenthetical meaning or a direct explanation link for king, and say which comparison guarantee is being borrowed or dropped. Do not add a survey of tournament algorithms.

locator.quote: a comparison has a fixed intended outcome

feedback.feedback: The distinction from earlier search methods is mathematically meaningful, but I would like the correspondence to the exposition’s two obstruction examples made explicit: a cycle defeats total-order intuition, while an unbiased loser comparison defeats a fixed bounded-error predicate interpretation.
feedback.why_it_matters: I may wrongly assume the cycle alone explains both limitations, or miss why the probabilistic comparison law matters beyond graph orientation.
feedback.advice: Point back to the two different conceptual obstructions using the existing examples and statements. Keep them separate instead of adding another historical paragraph.

locator.quote: We cite, and do not reprove,

feedback.feedback: This paragraph performs too many tasks at once: section roadmap, accepted-input boundary, optional refinements, meaning of record links and invitation to the exposition. Each part is useful, but the single dense paragraph is difficult to use as a route selector.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader does not know which jump is safe without retaining the full paragraph.
feedback.advice: Separate the route through the main argument from the compact statement of accepted inputs. Keep the existing precise list; give the exposition invitation its own clear entry point.

locator.section: 2. The Forrelation promise and the total function
locator.quote: All of these are independent input bits.

feedback.feedback: In a definition of a total function, independent can mean distinct freely assignable coordinates or stochastic independence under an input law. The latter is false for the planted distribution, where the selected transcripts and pointers depend on other fields. The exposition’s every assignment is allowed wording avoids this ambiguity.
feedback.why_it_matters: Probability becomes central in §4, so the reader may carry the wrong independence assumption into the lower-bound proof.
feedback.advice: Describe the fields as disjoint or freely assignable input coordinates here. Reserve probabilistic independence for the explicitly specified dummy experiment.

locator.section: 2. The Forrelation promise and the total function
locator.quote: so in terms of its input length $Q(F_{k,m})\le n^{1/44+o(1)}$.

feedback.feedback: This extra exponent arrives during the function definition, while the paper’s central comparison is R against Q rather than either against n. It is correct in context, but can divert a newcomer into a third exponent calculation before either main bound has been proved.
feedback.why_it_matters: The distinction between the size parameter m and actual input length n gets mixed with an optional quantitative consequence.
feedback.advice: Keep the exact input-length count and explain its role. Move this additional consequence to a short remark after the quantum estimate if it is needed for context.

locator.section: 2. The Forrelation promise and the total function / Local tests
locator.quote: and two output tests per transcript

feedback.feedback: A first reader may count the domain and value gates among S and then wonder why two more tests are added. The point is that one set checks the gate equations, while the extra tests demand the intended output values.
feedback.why_it_matters: The elementary count K acquires an unnecessary appearance of double counting.
